paper_title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observers motion, surrounding geometry, and handobject interactions must fit together in consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EGOXPERIENCE, full-stack * Equal contribution. Project leader. Data collection. Corresponding author. 1 paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EGOX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EGOX-Data-6M, 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EGOX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EGOX, trained with EGOX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in shared world coordinate frame with single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%. 1. Introduction Egocentric video offers natural perspective on how humans and embodied agents perceive and interact with the world, requiring only wearable camera without external camera setups. By capturing the wearers movement and close-range interactions, it provides visual cues for recovering camera pose, scene depth, hands, and objects. However, existing methods [58, 59, 25, 41, 73] typically recover only subset of these tightly coupled components. Combining outputs from different methods often requires reconciling inconsistent scales and coordinate frames, complicating their use in downstream embodied AI applications. This motivates unified feed-forward framework that jointly recovers the camera, scene, hands, and objects within single model. Training such unified model, however, requires large-scale egocentric data with joint annotations of the camera, scene, hands, and objects. Although egocentric video is easy to record, obtaining reliable joint annotations is considerably more difficult due to frequent hand-object occlusions, rapid head motion, and motion blur. Existing datasets [7, 3, 40, 12, 60] have made progress toward this goal, often using calibrated multi-camera or motion-capture systems to support reliable annotations. However, these systems require substantial setup and calibration, making collection difficult to scale across diverse real-world environments. Scaling jointly annotated egocentric data therefore calls for collection and annotation pipeline that reduces reliance on such specialized infrastructure. To address these challenges, we present EGOXPERIENCE, full-stack paradigm for egocentric 3D reconstruction, encompassing data collection, annotation, modeling, and benchmarking. Central to its annotation pipeline is EGOX-Engine, which tracks target objects across video frames and uses pre-scanned object models and observed depth to estimate and verify their 3D poses. SLAM-estimated camera poses place these object trajectories in shared world coordinate system alongside scene geometry and hand annotations, providing geometrically aligned supervision. Applying this engine to 50 hours of task-driven recordings spanning workspace manipulation, cross-room interactions, and outdoor loco-manipulation yields EGOX-Data-6M, further enriched with task captions at second-level temporal resolution. To complement this 2 dataset, we harmonize additional public interaction datasets [3, 40, 30, 60, 23, 12] under common training formulation, aligning their geometric conventions while retaining their partial annotations. We also establish EGOX-Bench from one hour of held-out recordings, enabling joint evaluation of camera, scene depth, hand, and object reconstruction across all capture settings. To translate this joint supervision into joint reconstruction, we introduce EGOX. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, EGOX jointly reconstructs the camera, scene depth, hands, and objects at metric scale in shared world coordinate system, all in single forward pass. During training, we supervise each component and additionally use the predicted camera poses to transform object and hand predictions into normalized world coordinates, where we supervise their positions and orientations. This ties camera, hand, and object estimation together, encouraging geometrically consistent reconstruction. Evaluated on four benchmarks, EGOX achieves state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space handobject pose recovery. It ranks first in depth, hand, and object metrics across all four benchmarks and achieves the best camera accuracy on HOI4D. Relative to the strongest competing methods, EgoX reduces camera nATE by 68.9% on HOI4D, hand W-MPJPE and depth AbsRel by 65.6% and 42.9% on EgoX-Bench, respectively, and improves object AUC-S50 by 28.0% on HOT3D. 2. Related Work 2.1. Scene and entity reconstruction DUSt3R [62] predicts pairwise pointmaps, while VGGT [58] jointly estimates cameras and scene geometry. CUT3R [61] introduces recurrent scene memory, and VGGT-Ω [59] reduces inter-frame attention through scene registers. Dynamic-scene methods recover moving geometry through world-space point tracking or temporally conditioned point prediction [72, 18, 57, 56, 70, 5]. Entity-aware models incorporate humans, instances, or hands into reconstruction: Human3R [14] jointly estimates human meshes, cameras, and scenes; HSImul3R [6] enables simulator-ready joint reconstruction of humans and scenes; IGGT [35] couples geometry with instance segmentation; and HGGT [38] estimates MANO parameters and cameras from uncalibrated views. EgoX extends this line of work to moving hands and manipulated objects, jointly reconstructing their motion, camera poses, and depth in shared metric frame. 2.2. Hand-object reconstruction HaMeR [46] and WiLoR [49] estimate MANO hand meshes from images. For world-space hand motion, HaWoR [71] combines hand reconstruction with SLAM and motion infilling, while Dyn-HaMR [69] uses camera tracking, motion priors, and test-time optimization. Hand3R [25], MINT [73], and ReViV [41] couple hand reconstruction with cameras or scene geometry; ReViV additionally predicts depth, body motion, and gaze. EgoX further incorporates manipulatedobject motion into the same feed-forward reconstruction. Keypoint Transformer [23] and HOPformer [4] estimate handobject interactions without recovering world-camera trajectory. HOLD [16] optimizes hand and object representations from video, while ForeHOI [13] completes object masks and shapes before geometric pose estimation. EgoGrasp [19] reconstructs hands and objects in separate stages, and WHOLE [66] requires object templates, metric camera trajectory, and test-time guidance. Related object-pose systems use CAD models, reference images, or RGB-D observations [31, 64, 32]. In contrast, EgoX jointly estimates camera poses, depth, hand geometry, and rigid-object poses from RGB observations and optional first-frame object masks. Table 1 Comparison of Egocentric Datasets. We compare data scale, capture settings, and annotation coverage. Obj. counts objects with 3D models.

Egocentric datasets and supervision HO-3D [22], DexYCB [12], H2O [30], H2O-3D [23], HOI4D [40], ARCTIC [17], HO-Cap [60], and HOT3D [3] provide hand-object annotations under different capture and geometric conventions. Recent datasets broaden scene coverage: SHOW3D [51] records indoor and outdoor interactions with mobile egoexo rig, Aria Digital Twin [45] provides scanned scenes and world-space trajectories, and HD-EPIC [47] captures unscripted activities with digital twins. Large corpora such as Ego4D [20], EPIC-KITCHENS [15], and EgoDex [24] provide broader human experience but more limited aligned geometric supervision. ACE-Data-0 [7] builds an ambient capture engine for calibrated and synchronized multimodal data collection in controlled environment. EgoX-Data-6M complements these resources with aligned camera, depth, hand, and object annotations across workspace manipulation, cross-area interaction, and outdoor locomotion. 3. The EGOXPERIENCE Paradigm Our EGOXPERIENCE unifies data capture, annotation and model learning for joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene depth, hands, and objects from egocentric videos. As illustrated in Fig. 1, this paradigm comprises EGOX-Engine for data processing and annotation (Sec. 3.1), EGOX-Data-6M with 50 hours of task-driven recordings spanning manipulation and locomotion (Sec. 3.2), and EGOX for joint reconstruction from monocular video (Sec. 3.3). 3.1. EGOX-Engine Learning to jointly reconstruct egocentric activity requires annotations that describe the camera, scene, hands, and objects in relation to one another. Obtaining these annotations is challenging because the observer and the interacting entities move simultaneously: change in image position may arise from camera motion, entity motion, or both. EGOX-Engine addresses this ambiguity by using stereo depth to recover geometry at metric scale and SLAM-estimated camera poses to align different annotations throughout each recording. This allows handobject motion to be expressed relative to the surrounding scene as the observer moves. Fig. 3 summarizes the overall pipeline. 4 Figure 2 Overview of EgoX-Data-6M. Examples and statistics summarize capture settings, task coverage, and aligned multimodal annotations. Capture and geometric reference. We record with the HOMIE Gen2 head-mounted rig [54], using its associated processing pipeline to estimate metric depth from the synchronized, calibrated front stereo pair and recover camera trajectories via SLAM from its four calibrated fisheye cameras. For each recording, we use the SLAM coordinate system as fixed session frame and transform camera-relative scene, hand, and object estimates into this frame. Object geometry and motion. Object annotation requires both geometric reference for each instance and its changing pose during interaction. We construct metric object meshes from 31 synchronized cameras mounted on calibrated dome. SAM 3 [11] then extracts object masks from the captured views, which are used for mesh reconstruction with MV-SAM3D [33]. To recover the objects physical dimensions, we put an AprilTag [44] board inside the dome to provide the scale reference. Given these metric object references, the engine recovers each objects motion in the egocentric recording. Specifically, we first identify the target object using first-frame mask and then specify the interaction interval over which to track it. Using the masked RGB image and its corresponding stereo depth, we estimate the initial pose of the pre-scanned object model in the camera frame. From this initial pose, we apply FoundationPose [64] to track the object throughout the specified interval, producing camera-relative pose sequence. We verify this sequence by checking whether the object model placed at the estimated pose agrees with the observed depth. Sequences that pass verification are transformed through the SLAM-estimated camera poses into the session frame, aligning object motion with the scene and hand annotations. Scene and hand annotations. The scene and hand annotations used in this alignment are derived from the same calibrated stereo observations. Specifically, we reconstruct scene geometry by back-projecting stereo depth and recover 3D hand keypoints through cross-view triangulation. We use these keypoints to constrain MANO fitting, with additional reprojection, depth, and temporal terms to refine the estimated hand geometry and motion. Hand shape parameters are shared across frames within each recording, while hand pose, position, and orientation are estimated independently for each frame. Finally, we transform the fitted hands and scene points through the camera trajectory into the session frame, placing them in the same metric coordinate system as the tracked objects. 5 Figure 3 Overview of EgoX-Engine. The pipeline converts egocentric recordings into structured multimodal annotations, including aligned geometry and temporally localized task captions. 3.2. EGOX-Data-6M Given EGOX-Engine, we apply it to annotate task-driven egocentric captures, constructing EGOX-Data-6M, which comprises 50 hours of video, 101 rigid objects, and 270 task scripts. The recordings cover activities ranging from manipulation within single workspace to interactions across rooms and loco-manipulation in outdoor environments. The engine provides geometrically aligned camera, scene, hand, and object annotations across these settings, supporting joint reconstruction under both local manipulation and extended movement. Fig. 2 illustrates the activity coverage and accompanying annotations. Task-driven collection. We organize data collection around task scripts, each specifying manipulation goal, target objects, and capture setting. Specifically, workspace scripts focus on local object manipulation, whereas cross-room and outdoor scripts incorporate movement between interaction locations. Annotation coverage. We provide geometric annotations in session-fixed metric frame, allowing camera motion, scene structure, and hand-object interactions to be related throughout each recording. Additionally, we include second-level task captions to describe the ongoing activity. Tab. 1 compares our dataset with existing egocentric resources. Compared with existing datasets, our EGOX-Data-6M brings together workspace manipulation, cross-room interactions, and outdoor locomotion with camera, scene, hand, and object annotations in shared metric frame, supporting joint reconstruction across these activity settings. Benchmark and complementary training data. To evaluate all reconstruction components on the same recordings, we reserve quality-controlled, one-hour subset spanning the three activity settings as EGOX-Bench. This subset is used exclusively for joint evaluation of camera, scene, hand, and object reconstruction. To broaden the training data beyond our own recordings, we incorporate additional public datasets. Using these datasets together requires accounting for differences in both geometric conventions and available annotations. We therefore convert their geometric labels to common coordinate and scale convention and supervise the model using the labels available in each dataset. This allows recordings with partial annotations to contribute to training without requiring every dataset to provide camera, scene, hand, and object labels. We also clean erroneous annotations and align depth with hand and object geometry to reduce conflicting supervision (Appendix B). Sec. 3.3 explains how the model learns from this combined supervision; the data mixture is detailed in Appendix F. 6 Figure 4 Overview of EgoX. Shared scene and entity features support joint reconstruction, while predicted cameras and scale place all outputs in common metric world frame. Figure 5 World-Space Hand and Camera Reconstruction. Qualitative comparisons on HOT3D and EgoX-Bench. Predictions and ground truth are shown in common world frame. 3.3. EGOX To translate the aligned supervision into joint reconstruction, we propose EGOX, which is capable of predicting the camera, scene, and motions of both hands and objects within single model. The central challenge to achieve this goal is that the predictions must agree geometrically as both the viewpoint and interaction change. As illustrated in Fig. 4, we address this through joint scene and entity representation, followed by explicit composition through the predicted camera poses. Supervision on the resulting hand and object motions then ties their reconstruction to camera estimation. Problem formulation. Given monocular observations = {𝐼𝑡}𝑇 𝑡=1 and optional first-frame object masks = {𝐵1, 𝑗}𝑁 𝑗=1 identifying the target objects, EGOX jointly predicts camera intrinsics and poses, dense depth, two-hand MANO states, object origins and orientations, and positive metric scale in single forward pass. We express all reconstructed outputs in W, the coordinate system of the first-frame camera. For those complementary datasets without ground-truth object masks, we adopt the pipeline to reconstruct only cameras, scene geometry, and hands. 7 Figure 6 Camera-Frame Object Pose Reconstruction. Qualitative comparisons of object 6-DoF predictions with ground truth on HOT3D and EgoX-Bench. Figure 7 Depth Reconstruction. GT: refined official depth. VGGT/VGGT-Ω: one scale fitted to DA3 Nested depth per sequence; others: predicted metric scale. Joint scene and entity representation. To jointly estimate cameras, scene geometry, and handobject motion, we encode them with shared Transformer. Starting from image patch features extracted by DINOv3 [55], we introduce camera, hand, and object tokens in each view, using distinct left/right embeddings to identify the hands and first-frame mask descriptors to associate target objects across views. These tokens gather image evidence through within-view attention and exchange information across observations through cross-view attention, forming joint representation for reconstruction. Architectural details are provided in Appendix F. Reconstruction in shared metric frame. From the joint representation, we reconstruct scene geometry and hand-object motion in common reference frame W, defined by the first-frame camera coordinate system. To combine predictions across views, we estimate camera intrinsics ˆ𝐾𝑡 and extrinsics ( ˆ𝑅𝑡, ˆ𝜏𝑡) mapping to camera 𝑡. These parameters allow us to recover scene points, wrist positions, and object origins from their image coordinates and predicted depths. Specifically, for homogeneous image position 𝑢 = (𝑢𝑥, 𝑢𝑦, 1) and normalized depth 𝑧, its position in is: U𝑡 ( 𝑢, 𝑧) = ˆ𝑅 𝑡 𝑧 ˆ𝐾 1 𝑡 𝑢 ˆ𝜏𝑡 (cid:16) (cid:17) . (1) This shared mapping ties scene and entity positions to the same camera estimates. For hand and object orientations, we similarly use inverse camera rotation ˆ𝑅 𝑡 to transform camera-frame hand and object orientations into W, keeping MANO joint rotations local and expressing object rotations relative to their first-frame orientations. The reconstruction in obtained above still uses normalized depths and translations. For hands, this adjusts only the wrist positions while preserving the metric dimensions of the MANO meshes. Geometrically coupled supervision. Building on this shared reconstruction, we supervise not only individual predictions but also the resulting hand-object geometry in W. To compute this geometric supervision, we transform hand and object predictions through the estimated cameras and compare the reconstructed geometry with ground truth. The resulting loss backpropagates through the camera transformations, updating both entity and camera predictions. We combine these supervision terms into the training objective: = Llocal + Ldense + Lcoupled + Lscale, (2) where Llocal supervises camera and view-local entity predictions, Ldense supervises depth and scene points, Lcoupled supervises the composed hand-object geometry, and Lscale supervises metric scale. To accommodate varying annotation coverage across datasets, we apply each loss only where its required labels are available, allowing fully and partially annotated data to contribute to the same objective. Loss definitions and training settings are provided in Appendix F. 4. Experiments We evaluate camera, depth, hand, and object reconstruction on HOT3D, EgoX-Bench, H2O, and HOI4D using identical 150-observation clips across methods. Evaluation sequences are excluded from EgoX training. EgoX uses RGB and first-frame object masks; object baselines may additionally require estimated depth, intrinsics, per-frame masks, or metric CAD assets. Worldspace hand metrics use estimated cameras; object poses are evaluated in camera coordinates. No method receives GT camera poses or scale in the main comparisons. Evaluation scope The evaluated methods cover different subsets of the reconstruction problem. Table 2 summarizes their outputs and inference structure. Subsequent comparisons therefore evaluate each method only on the outputs it provides under the matched protocol described above. EgoX is the only end-to-end method in this comparison that jointly reconstructs cameras, depth, hands, and object 6-DoF poses in shared world frame. 4.2. Main results World-space hands. EgoX achieves the lowest PA-, WA-, and W-MPJPE on all four benchmarks  (Table 3)  . On HOT3D, it reduces W-MPJPE from 56.30 to 38.89 mm relative to HaWoR, the strongest baseline on this metric, despite HaWoRs adaptive DROID-SLAM and Metric3D-based scale [71]. On EgoX-Bench, W-MPJPE falls from 328.81 mm for WiLoR + SLAM to 113.24 mm. Figure 5 illustrates improved world-space placement: baseline hands recover plausible local hand poses but exhibit large deviations from the ground-truth positions in world coordinates, whereas EgoX closely matches the ground truth. Object 6-DoF. EgoX achieves the best ADD, ADD-S, and AUC-S50 on all four benchmarks  (Table 4)  . On EgoX-Bench, its AUC-S50 is 76.59, compared with 59.80 for GigaPose + MegaPose, 10 Table 6 ScaleHead Ablation. Results on HOT3D with predicted (P) or oracle (G) scale. Table 7 DepthHead Ablation. Results on HOT3D with predicted scale in both settings. Setting 𝑠 AUC-S50 AbsRel 38.89 w/ head w/o head 40.67 73.71 60.87 0.0604 0.0620 Setting 𝑠 AUC-S50 AbsRel 38.89 w/ head w/o head 67.53 73.71 41.09 0.0604 N/A the strongest competing result, although that pipeline additionally uses metric CAD assets and per-frame masks. EgoX also outperforms Any6D on HOI4D, where Any6D receives estimated depth, intrinsics, and per-frame masks. These comparisons show more accurate camera-frame poses with fewer auxiliary inputs (Appendix C). Figure 6 shows larger translation or rotation offsets for the object baselines, while EgoX more closely matches the ground-truth pose. Camera motion. Compared with ReViV, which also reconstructs cameras, depth, and hands, EgoX achieves lower nATE and RRE on all four benchmarks  (Table 5)  . On HOI4D, EgoX also leads the geometry baselines: nATE is 0.0066 versus 0.0212 for VGGT-Ω, and RRE is 0.78 versus 1.50 for VGGT. VGGT-Ω leads on HOT3D and EgoX-Bench, while DA3 Nested leads on H2O. VGGT-Ωs camera advantage may reflect its large-scale geometric training on diverse static and dynamic scenes [59]. Depth reconstruction. EgoX achieves the lowest AbsRel and highest 𝛿1.25 on all four benchmarks  (Table 5)  . On EgoX-Bench, AbsRel is 0.0460 versus 0.3972 for ReViV and 0.0806 for VGGT-Ω; 𝛿1.25 is 97.37 versus 91.57 for VGGT-Ω. EgoX obtains these results with its own predicted metric scale, while VGGT-Ω uses scale estimated from DA3 Nested depth (Section C). The results support accurate metric depth alongside hand and object reconstruction. Figure 7 shows that EgoX better matches the refined ground-truth depth. 4.3. Ablation studies Metric scale prediction. We remove ScaleHead and use oracle scale (G) to convert the ablated models predictions to metric units. Despite this advantage, W-MPJPE increases from 38.89 to 40.67 mm and AUC-S50 decreases from 73.71 to 60.87  (Table 6)  , showing that ScaleHead benefits joint reconstruction beyond final rescaling. Dense-depth prediction. We remove DepthHead while retaining the remaining architecture and predicted scale. W-MPJPE increases to 67.53 mm and AUC-S50 decreases to 41.09  (Table 7)  , showing that explicit depth prediction improves hand and object reconstruction through the shared representation. 5. Conclusion We present EgoXperience, unified approach to learning world-grounded egocentric representations through task-driven capture, geometrically aligned annotation, and joint reconstruction. EgoX-Engine provides aligned multimodal annotations for the 50-hour EgoX-Data-6M, from which we curate the held-out one-hour EgoX-Bench. Trained on these annotations and harmonized public datasets, EgoX jointly reconstructs cameras, dense depth, hands, and rigid-object 6-DoF poses in common metric world frame. Experiments on EgoX-Bench and public benchmarks demonstrate strong performance in hand and object reconstruction and depth estimation. Our current formulation assumes rigid objects and does not predict their meshes. Future work will explore object mesh prediction and multiview inputs.

sections.title: F Training and Compute
sections.content: 18 18 18 18 19 19 20 20 20 21 22 17 A. Extended Related Work A.1. Joint geometry and entity reconstruction DUSt3R [62] predicts pairwise pointmaps, while VGGT [58] jointly estimates cameras and geometry. CUT3R [61] uses recurrent scene memory, and VGGT-Ω [59] reduces inter-frame attention costs with scene registers. EgoX combines register-mediated and global attention with hand, object, and scale tokens. For dynamic scenes, MonST3R [72] reconstructs moving content, and St4RTrack [18] tracks 3D points in common world frame. Dynamic Point Maps [57] recovers rigid-object motion through masked point alignment, V-DPM [56] extends pointmaps to video, and D4RT [70] predicts 3D points conditioned on source, target, and camera-reference times. EgoX directly predicts articulated hands and rigid object poses alongside cameras and depth. Human3R [14] combines human meshes with scene and camera reconstruction, while IGGT [35] jointly learns geometry and instance segmentation. HGGT [38] uses hand tokens to estimate MANO parameters and cameras from uncalibrated views of fixed hand configuration. Unlike these methods, EgoX jointly reconstructs the camera, depth, and moving hands and objects over time. A.2. Hand and handobject reconstruction HaMeR [46] regresses MANO [52] parameters from hand crops, while WiLoR [49] pairs hand detection with mesh estimation. For world-space motion, HaWoR [71] combines hand reconstruction with SLAM and motion infilling; Dyn-HaMR [69] uses camera tracking, motion priors, and optimization. Hand3R [25] couples hand estimator with recurrent scene modeling, while MINT [73] and ReViV [41] jointly estimate hand and camera motion, with ReViV also modeling depth, body motion, and gaze. EgoX additionally predicts manipulated-object motion. Simulation-ready objects [810] and synthetic motion [27, 68] enable interaction data at scale, but may not capture natural human manipulation. Keypoint Transformer [23] and HOPformer [4] estimate handobject interactions without world-camera trajectory. HOLD [16] optimizes hand and object representations from video; ForeHOI [13] completes masks and shapes before geometrically estimating object poses, without requiring separate input masks. ArtHOI [63] handles articulated objects, whereas EgoX models rigid objects. For world-space interactions, EgoGrasp [19] reconstructs hands and objects in separate stages. WHOLE [66] uses motion prior and test-time guidance but requires object templates and metric camera trajectory. EgoX jointly predicts cameras, depth, hands, and objects from RGB video and initial object masks, without either external input. Its reconstruction losses evaluate hand, object, and depth predictions through the predicted camera, providing training signals for camera estimation. A.3. Camera, depth, and object-pose pipelines Modular reconstruction also provides source of training annotations. MegaSaM [36] and ViPE [26] combine learned geometry with camera and depth optimization. Metric3D [67] and UniDepth [48] predict metric depth from single images, while MapAnything [29] predicts metric geometry from multiple views. HaWoR uses metric depth to scale its SLAM trajectory. EgoX instead learns scale per window shared by depth and camera, hand, and object translations, though shared scale alone does not ensure geometric consistency. MegaPose [31] requires CAD model, FoundationPose [64] accepts model or reference images, and Any6D [32] uses an RGB-D reference. Their camera-relative poses can be mapped 18 to world coordinates using camera trajectory. EgoX likewise transforms predictions into common frame, but learns camera and object estimates jointly. These methods also differ in their requirements for depth, pose initialization, scale, and masks. A.4. Datasets and geometric evaluation HO-3D [22], DexYCB [12], H2O [30], H2O-3D [23], HOI4D [40], ARCTIC [17], TACO [39], HOCap [60], and HOT3D [3] support handobject reconstruction under varied capture protocols. ARCTIC includes articulated objects, and HOT3D provides motion-capture reference poses. However, capture volumes or clip protocols often limit evaluation of continuous camera travel between workspaces. More recent datasets broaden the settings. SHOW3D [51] captures indoor and outdoor interactions with mobile egoexo rig, but defines annotations relative to the moving rig. EPIC-Contact [4] provides fitted meshes and contact correspondences in kitchen video. Aria Digital Twin [45] provides camera and object trajectories, scanned scenes, and rendered depth; HD-EPIC [47] provides unscripted kitchen recordings with digital twins and 3D object motion, though its labels serve different purpose from dense hand and object pose trajectories. Large collections such as Ego4D [20] and EPIC-KITCHENS [15] support learned geometric supervision. EgoDex [24] scales manipulation data, while MINT [73] builds camera-and-hand corpus through automatic annotation. Our data spans workspace manipulation, travel between indoor workspaces, and outdoor locomotion, with hand, object, and scene annotations. This enables evaluation across camera displacement, capture setting, and sequence duration using camera, depth, and world-space interaction errors. B. Public Dataset Cleaning and Geometric Alignment We systematically clean HOT3D, HOI4D, H2O, H2O-3D, HO-Cap, and DexYCB before joint training. We discard frames with erroneous hand annotations and remove spurious points from depth-derived point clouds. We further align depth-derived geometry, MANO hand meshes, and object meshes in common 3D coordinate system, correcting inconsistencies in their relative placement and scale. These steps reduce erroneous labels and conflicting geometric supervision across reconstruction tasks. C. Evaluation Protocol Datasets and splits. We evaluate on four sequence-disjoint benchmarks: HaWoRs validation split of HOT3D [71], the held-out one-hour EgoX-Bench, the official H2O test split, and our sequence-level HOI4D validation split. Evaluation sequences are excluded from EgoX training. All methods use identical sequence lists and matched 150-observation clips. Inputs and matched protocol. EgoX receives RGB and optional first-frame object masks. Object-pose baselines additionally use DA3 Nested depth and intrinsics, per-frame masks, or metric CAD assets as required; their runtimes include any required DA3 preprocessing. We combine the EgoX-Data-6M training split with six independently sourced public interaction datasets: HOT3D [3], HOI4D [40], H2O [30], HO-Cap [60], H2O3D [23], and DexYCB [12]. We reprocess them so that depth, hand geometry, and object geometry agree under consistent metric camera conventions, avoiding contradictory supervision across tasks. Additional real-world sources are Xperience-10M [53], ACE-Data-0 [7], and AgiBot World 2026 [1]; synthetic sources are Aria Synthetic Environments [2], BEHAVIOR-1K [34], SceneNet RGB-D [42], and Dynamic Replica [28]. The pool contains approximately 280 hours. Training first mixes real and synthetic sources and then continues on an equal mixture of the retained real interaction sources. We sample 𝑇 {1, . . . , 24} observations per input set. Architecture details. Patch features from DINOv3 ViT-L/16 feed 24-block reconstruction Transformer with hidden dimension of 1024. Nineteen blocks exchange all tokens across views, while the remaining five operate on compact register and entity tokens. Camera and depth heads read fused image features, whereas hand and object heads read their view-specific entity states. The model uses learned spatial and reference embeddings without temporal encoding. Coordinate and scale conventions. Training uses common normalization factor 𝑧gt, defined as the mean Euclidean distance of valid metric depth points from the reference-camera origin after transformation into W. Metric depth and translations are divided by 𝑧gt; rotations and intrinsics are unchanged. For wrist-centred MANO joints ˆ𝐽𝑚 rel,𝑡 and reconstructed wrist ˆ𝑤𝑛 𝑡 , training-space and metric joints are ˆ𝐽𝑛 𝑡 = ˆ𝐽𝑚 rel,𝑡 𝑧gt + ˆ𝑤𝑛 𝑡 , ˆ𝐽𝑚 𝑡 = ˆ𝐽𝑚 rel,𝑡 + ˆ𝑠 ˆ𝑤𝑛 𝑡 . The parameter term applies ℓ1 losses to normalized camera translation, standardized unit quaternions, field of view, and normalized principal point; geodesic losses to hand and object rotations; Smooth L1 losses to MANO shape, image positions, and log-depths; and class-weighted binary cross-entropy to in-frame predictions. Image-position residuals are normalized by the longer image dimension. Ground-truth cameras define the view-local targets. The dense losses L𝐷 and L𝑃 follow VGGT-Ω, combining confidence-weighted residuals, inverse-depth weighting, confidence regularization, and multiscale gradient penalties. Hand and object reconstruction use Smooth L1 penalties after composition through predicted cameras. Object rotation uses 𝑑sym( 𝐴, 𝐵) = min𝐺 S𝑟 𝑑( 𝐴, 𝐵𝐺), where 𝑑 is geodesic distance and S𝑟 is the objects symmetry group in the reference orientation. The reference rotation is supervised toward identity without symmetry relaxation; the coupled term applies to non-reference views. All reductions use annotation-validity and in-frame masks, and object terms additionally require bound reference mask. Missing annotations are not treated as negative labels. Sampling and optimization. The source composition and two-stage mixture are summarized above. Each per-GPU batch samples 𝑇 {1, . . . , 24} and uses 𝑇-dependent batch size to maintain an approximately constant image budget. The image encoder is initialized from pretrained DINOv3 weights and the remaining modules randomly. All modules are optimized jointly using AdamW with linear warm-up, cosine decay, mixed precision, and module-wise gradient clipping.
